A changed name expresses an argument about loss

Naomi returns to a town that still knows her name (verse 19). She asks to be called Mara, and the verse ties that name to bitterness. She blames the Almighty directly in verses 20–21. She left full, she says, and the LORD brought her back empty. Ruth stands beside her as she says “empty.” The book lets the complaint stand without any rebuke. Verse 22 then quietly adds two things: Ruth and the harvest.
A harvest rule becomes a means of survival

The law left the edges of a field for the poor and the foreigner. Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 state the rule. Ruth is both, and in verse 7 she still asks permission. Verses 9 and 22 show why: a woman alone in a field risked harm. Boaz first gives what the law requires and then more. He orders his men to pull stalks out for her (verse 16). In verse 20 Naomi’s speech changes, and she blesses the LORD’s kindness.
Ruth gives the plan her own words

Naomi’s plan ends with Boaz telling Ruth what to do (verse 4). In verse 9 Ruth tells Boaz what to do. She asks for his covering and gives the reason: he is a near kinsman. That ties her marriage to his family duty toward Naomi’s house. In 2:12 Boaz prayed that the LORD would shelter her. Now she asks him to be that shelter. Boaz calls her request a kindness and names her a worthy woman (verses 10–11).

The gate is the town’s court, and ten elders make the act public. The nearer kinsman accepts the field (verse 4) and refuses Ruth (verse 6). A son by Ruth would carry Mahlon’s name and inherit the land. Boaz accepts that cost in verses 9–10 before witnesses. The man who guarded his own estate is never named in the book. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale. The women tell Naomi that Ruth is better than seven sons (verse 15).
